concept_graph.summary: Fluent speakers of a language bring an enormous amount of knowledge to bear during comprehension and production, with vocabulary being a useful lens to explore the acquisition of knowledge from text. The vocabulary is embodied in many forms, perhaps most obviously in the vocabulary, the rich representations we have of words and their meanings and usage. Fluent young adults possess between 30,000 and 100,000 words.

A language model is simply a computational system that can predict the next word from previous words, given a context or prefix of words. A language model assigns a probability distribution over the possible next words. Language models can predict words from the previous word or handful of words.

Pretraining is the process of learning knowledge about language and the world from iteratively predicting tokens in vast amounts of text. This process makes large language models possible, allowing them to learn all this knowledge of language, context, and the world simply by being taught to predict the next word, again and again, based on context.

A large language model is just a larger version of what we’ve seen before, with the ability to predict words given contexts of thousands or even tens of thousands of words. Large language models can learn all this knowledge of language, context, and the world simply by being taught to predict the next word, again and again, based on context, in a very large corpus of text.

A language model assigns a probability distribution over the possible next words, given a context or prefix of words. This distribution is a key component of language models, allowing them to predict the next word in a sequence.

The distributional hypothesis posits that we derive meaning from the company words keep, by analyzing which words frequently co-occur. This theory allows us to build complex maps of meaning from text alone, even without direct real-world experience, and is a key component of large language models.
